newsitem.title: UK: UK's Ashdown dismisses Lib-Lab election pact talk.
newsitem.headline: UK's Ashdown dismisses Lib-Lab election pact talk.

text.p: British Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown on Monday dismissed suggestions that his minority party had struck up an electoral pact with the main opposition Labour Party.

Ashdown denied comments by a BBC interviewer that his party's talks with Labour on constitutional reform -- described by Prime Minister John Major as "profoundly dangerous" -- amounted to a putatative electoral coalition alliance.
"It is rubbish if they say that because the Liberal Democrats have different policies from Labour. We are opposed to windfall tax for example," Ashdown told BBC radio in an interview.
Labour and Liberal Democrat plans to push through a wide-ranging package of constitutional reforms if they win power, has fuelled a ferocious assault by the Conservatives.
Major has used news of the talks to claim that the two parties are now effectively locked together.

Ashdown said he had not even discussed the possibility with Labour's Tony Blair of the Liberal Democrats sharing power with Labour should there be an inconclusive result in general elections, which must be held by May.
"All that is for the other side of the election. Everything is possible (but) if you want me to make a judgement about it, it is exceedingly unlikely," Ashdown said.
Ashdown noted he had made clear the Liberal Democrats would be prepared in principle to work with other parties after the election.
"If we can work with others...across the floor of the House of Commons in order to provide a better future for our country of course we shall do so," he said.

Conservative MP Hugh Dykes, a prominent pro-European, said he had agreed to have talks with the Labour-Liberal Democrat committee considering constitutional reforms. His decision is likely to embarass the Conservative leadership.
Dykes told BBC radio he was interested in discussions on reforming Parliament's upper House of Lords and changing the voting system in the European Union.
Conservative Party chairman Brian Mawhinney shrugged off Dykes decision, saying he was not one of the party's senior MPs.
"MPs talk to each other all the time about a variety of things," Mawhinney told BBC radio.
